prose_changes.new: The Caves Monastery survived the sack and is still there. Today it is the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, with underground passages full of relics, and one of the great monasteries of the Orthodox world. In our own century it is also claimed by rival Ukrainian churches. The writings this church left, above all the Primary Chronicle, are the founding record of East Slavic history. Boris and Gleb, princes honored as saints because they did not fight back, set a pattern of holiness of their own among the Slavs. Who inherits Kyiv's legacy — Kyiv, Moscow, or both — is a live political question to this day. The century of Mongol rule after 1240 left few records. What ran through it was the see of the metropolitan. It moved north to Vladimir and then to Moscow, and Moscow later claimed Kyiv's legacy as its own.

Carried by the new Documented gave-rise-to link to Muscovite Christianity. The thin record of the Mongol century is kept. The 46-word sentence is split. The paragraph is rewritten whole for reading level (Reading Ease 36); every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: In July 1054 a papal legate laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and walked out. The patriarch, Michael Cerularius, condemned him in return. Neither man believed he had divided Christendom, and for a long time nobody treated the breach as final. But the estrangement between the Greek and Latin churches did not heal, and it hardened catastrophically in 1204, when a crusading army sacked Constantinople, installed a Latin patriarch, and drove the imperial church into exile at Nicaea for nearly sixty years. The Byzantines returned in 1261. In 1274, needing Western help against his enemies, Emperor Michael VIII accepted union with Rome at the Second Council of Lyon.
